sentences.text: Mirischia was a small bipedal predator that lived in northeastern Brazil during the Early Cretaceous.

The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — includes a partial articulated skeleton with the pelvis, incomplete hind limbs, vertebrae, ribs, and thigh bones, all of which exhibit an exceptionally thin bone wall.
Estimates from 2004 and 2010 suggest the animal measured 2.1 meters in length and weighed seven kilograms.
The specific name asymmetrica refers to the asymmetry between the left and right ischium in the fossil specimen, where the left bone has an oval hole and the right bone has an open notch.
A piece of petrified intestine was preserved in front of the pubic bones of the holotype.
The specimen preserves soft tissue remains, including a vacuity interpreted as an air sac between the pubic and ischial bones.
The species Mirischia asymmetrica was named and described in 2004 by David Martill, Eberhard Frey, and Darren Naish.

In 2004, Mirischia was classified within the Compsognathidae family, but later suggestions placed it as a basal member of the Tyrannosauroidea or in a polytomy within basal Coelurosauria, excluding it from the Compsognathus genus.
Mirischia lived between 119.57 and 113.2 million years ago during the Aptian stage.
